latin: non possum reticere, deae, qua me Allius in re
english: I cannot keep silent, goddesses, in what matter me Allius
note: deae: the Muses. Allius is Merrill's reading of the friend's name (other editors Manlius or Mallius).

latin: iuverit aut quantis iuverit officiis,
english: helped, or with how great services he helped,

latin: ne fugiens saeclis obliviscentibus aetas
english: lest fleeing time, with forgetting generations,
note: saeclis obliviscentibus: ablative absolute, 'as the ages forget'.

latin: illius hoc caeca nocte tegat studium:
english: may cover this zeal of his in blind night:
note: illius ... studium: his devoted service.

latin: sed dicam vobis, vos porro dicite multis
english: but I will tell you, you in turn tell many

latin: milibus et facite haec charta loquatur anus
english: thousands, and make this page speak, an old woman,
note: charta ... anus: anus used as an adjective, 'the paper when grown old', i.e. in ages to come.
A line is lost in the manuscripts here; the gap marker is kept.

latin: notescatque magis mortuus atque magis,
english: and may he become known more, dead, and more,
note: magis ... atque magis: more and more after his death.

latin: nec tenuem texens sublimis aranea telam
english: nor, weaving its thin web, the high-hanging spider

latin: in deserto Alli nomine opus faciat.
english: on the deserted name of Allius do its work.
note: Metaphor: may his name never lie neglected under cobwebs, i.e. be forgotten.

latin: nam mihi quam dederit duplex Amathusia curam
english: For what care to me the double-dealing Amathusian gave
note: Amathusia: Venus, from Amathus in Cyprus; duplex 'twofold', i.e. deceitful, or giving both joy and pain.

latin: scitis, et in quo me corruerit genere,
english: you know, and in what manner she overthrew me,
note: corruerit: brought me down, ruined me.

latin: cum tantum arderem quantum Trinacria rupes
english: when I burned as much as the Trinacrian rock
note: Trinacria rupes: Etna in Sicily.

latin: lymphaque in Oetaeis Malia Thermopylis,
english: and the Malian water in Oetaean Thermopylae,
note: The hot springs at Thermopylae near Mount Oeta and the Malian gulf.

latin: maesta neque adsiduo tabescere lumina fletu
english: and my sad eyes neither from constant weeping to waste away
note: neque ... cessarent: the eyes did not cease to waste away, (and) the cheeks (did not cease) to be wet.

latin: cessarent tristique imbre madere genae,
english: ceased, and with sad rain to be wet my cheeks,
note: imbre: shower, i.e. tears.

latin: qualis in aerii perlucens vertice montis
english: such as, shining clear on the top of a lofty mountain,
note: Simile: the stream may illustrate the flowing tears (15-16) or the relief Allius brought (23-26); commentators divide.

latin: rivus muscoso prosilit e lapide,
english: a stream leaps out from a mossy stone,

latin: qui, cum de prone praeceps est valle volutus,
english: which, when headlong down the sloping valley it has rolled,
note: prone: Merrill's spelling for prona, 'sloping'.

latin: per medium densi transit iter populi,
english: crosses through the middle of the road of a dense people,
note: densi populi: crowded with people.

latin: dulce viatori lasso in sudore levamen
english: a sweet relief to the traveller weary in his sweat,

latin: cum gravis exustos aestus hiulcat agros.
english: when heavy heat cracks open the burnt-up fields.

latin: hic, velut in nigro iactatis turbine nautis
english: Here, as to sailors tossed in a black whirlwind

latin: lenius adspirans aura secunda venit
english: breathing more gently a favouring breeze comes,

latin: iam prece Pollucis, iam Castoris implorata,
english: implored now by prayer of Pollux, now of Castor,
note: prece Pollucis ... Castoris: prayer to Pollux and Castor, protectors of sailors.

latin: tale fuit nobis Allius auxilium.
english: such a help to us was Allius.

latin: is clausum lato patefecit limite campum,
english: He opened a closed field with a broad path,
note: Metaphor: he gave access to a love that had been shut off to the poet; limes is a boundary-path.

latin: isque domum nobis isque dedit dominae,
english: and he a house to us, and he gave to a mistress,
note: dominae: to my mistress (Lesbia), or the 'mistress' of the house; disputed.

latin: ad quam communes exerceremus amores.
english: at which we might practise our shared loves.
note: quam: feminine, referring to domum (house) of line 28.

latin: quo mea se molli candida diva pede
english: whither my radiant goddess with soft foot herself
note: candida diva: the beloved (Lesbia).

latin: intulit et trito fulgentem in limine plantam
english: brought, and on the worn threshold her shining sole

latin: innixa arguta constituit solea,
english: resting, set it down with a creaking sandal,
note: arguta solea: sandal that squeaks or clicks; treading on the threshold was an omen.

latin: coniugis ut quondam flagrans advenit amore
english: as once, burning with love of her husband, came

latin: Protesilaeam Laodamia domum
english: to the Protesilaean house Laodamia,
note: Laodamia, bride of Protesilaus, the first Greek killed at Troy.

latin: inceptam frustra, nondum cum sanguine sacro
english: begun in vain, when not yet with sacred blood

latin: hostia caelestis pacificasset eros.
english: a victim had appeased the heavenly masters.
note: eros: accusative plural of erus, 'masters', i.e. the gods; the proper sacrifice before building the house was omitted.

latin: nil mihi tam valde placeat, Rhamnusia virgo,
english: Let nothing please me so greatly, Rhamnusian virgin,
note: Rhamnusia virgo: Nemesis, worshipped at Rhamnus in Attica.

latin: quod temere invitis suscipiatur eris.
english: that it would be undertaken rashly with the masters unwilling.
note: eris: the gods, as in line 36.

latin: quam ieiuna pium desideret ara cruorem
english: how the fasting altar longs for pious blood

latin: docta est amisso Laodamia viro,
english: Laodamia learned, her husband lost,

latin: coniugis ante coacta novi dimittere collum
english: forced before to let go the neck of her new husband
note: ante ... quam (41-42): 'before ... than', i.e. before one winter and another had sated her love.

latin: quam veniens una atque altera rursus hiems
english: than, coming one and another again, winter

latin: noctibus in longis avidum saturasset amorem,
english: in long nights had sated her greedy love,

latin: posset ut abrupto vivere coniugio:
english: so that she could live with marriage broken off:

latin: quod scibant Parcae non longo tempore abesse,
english: which the Fates knew to be not a long time away,
note: non longo tempore abesse: 'to be not far off' (his death).

latin: si miles muros isset ad Iliacos:
english: if as a soldier he had gone to the Ilian walls:
note: Iliacos: of Ilium, Troy.

latin: nam tum Helenae raptu primores Argivorum
english: for then by the seizure of Helen the foremost of the Argives
note: raptu: abduction, carrying off.

latin: coeperat ad sese Troia ciere viros,
english: Troy had begun to summon to itself, men,
note: primores ... viros (47-48): the foremost men of the Argives.

latin: Troia (nefas) commune sepulcrum Asiae Europaeque,
english: Troy (horror!) the common tomb of Asia and Europe,
note: nefas: unspeakable thing; the parenthesis is in the Latin.

latin: Troia virum et virtutum omnium acerba cinis:
english: Troy the bitter ash of men and of all virtues:
note: virum: genitive plural of vir; cinis here feminine (acerba).

latin: quaene etiam nostro letum miserabile fratri
english: which also to our brother a pitiful death
note: quaene: Merrill's reading, an emphatic relative ('which indeed'); others read quae nunc or quae vetet. nostro: 'our' for 'my'.

latin: attulit. Hei misero frater adempte mihi,
english: brought. Alas, brother taken from wretched me,

latin: hei misero fratri iucundum lumen ademptum,
english: alas, a pleasant light taken from a wretched brother,
note: iucundum lumen: the light of life, or (for the poet) the joy of his life; misero fratri is dative.

latin: tecum una tota est nostra sepulta domus,
english: with you together all our house is buried,

latin: omnia tecum una perierunt gaudia nostra,
english: all with you together have perished our joys,

latin: quae tuus in vita dulcis alebat amor.
english: which your sweet love in life used to nourish.

latin: quem nunc tam longe non inter nota sepulcra
english: whom now so far away not among known tombs

latin: nec prope cognatos compositum cineres,
english: nor laid to rest near kindred ashes,

latin: sed Troia obscena, Troia infelice sepultum
english: but buried in Troy the obscene, Troy the unlucky,
note: obscena: ill-omened, accursed.

latin: detinet extremo terra aliena solo.
english: a foreign land holds back in a farthest soil.
note: extremo solo: at the end of the earth.

latin: ad quam tum properans fertur simul undique pubes
english: to which then, hastening together from everywhere, is said the youth
note: fertur (61) governs deseruisse (62): 'is said to have deserted'.

latin: Graeca penetralis deseruisse focos,
english: of Greece to have deserted their inner hearths,
note: penetralis focos: the hearths of the inner house.

latin: ne Paris abducta gavisus libera moecha
english: lest Paris, rejoicing in the carried-off adulteress, free
note: libera agrees with otia (64): 'free leisure'. moecha: adulteress (Helen).

latin: otia pacato degeret in thalamo.
english: leisure should spend in a peaceful bedchamber.

latin: quo tibi tum casu, pulcherrima Laodamia,
english: By which mischance then from you, most beautiful Laodamia,

latin: ereptum est vita dulcius atque anima
english: was snatched, sweeter than life and soul,

latin: coniugium: tanto te absorbens vertice amoris
english: your marriage: in so great a whirlpool of love swallowing you
note: vertice: whirlpool, eddy.

latin: aestus in abruptum detulerat barathrum,
english: the surge had carried down into a sheer abyss,
note: Metaphor: her love as a flood sweeping her into an abyss.

latin: quale ferunt Grai Pheneum prope Cylleneum
english: such as the Greeks say near Cyllenean Pheneus

latin: siccare emulsa pingue palude solum,
english: dries, the marsh drained off, the rich soil,
note: siccare: infinitive after ferunt (the Greeks say [it] dries); the drained marsh at Pheneus in Arcadia, below Mount Cyllene.

latin: quod quondam caesis montis fodisse medullis
english: which once, the marrow of the mountain cut, to have dug
note: medullis: marrow, i.e. the heart of the mountain.

latin: audit falsiparens Amphitryoniades,
english: is said the falsely-fathered son of Amphitryon,
note: audit: 'is spoken of as having dug'. falsiparens Amphitryoniades: Hercules, whose putative father Amphitryon was not his true father (Jupiter).

latin: tempore quo certa Stymphalia monstra sagitta
english: at the time when with sure arrow the Stymphalian monsters
note: The Stymphalian birds.

latin: perculit imperio deterioris eri,
english: he struck down at the command of a worse master,
note: deterioris eri: Eurystheus.

latin: pluribus ut caeli tereretur ianua divis,
english: so that by more gods the door of heaven might be worn,
note: Hercules is to be deified, adding to the gods who tread heaven's threshold.

latin: Hebe nec longa virginitate foret.
english: and Hebe not in long virginity might be.
note: Hebe becomes Hercules' wife in heaven.

latin: sed tuus altus amor barathro fuit altior illo,
english: But your deep love was deeper than that abyss,

latin: qui tunc indomitam ferre iugum docuit.
english: which then taught the untamed one to bear the yoke.
note: qui: masculine, = amor. indomitam: feminine, Laodamia. iugum: the yoke of marriage (metaphor).

latin: nam nec tam carum confecto aetate parenti
english: For neither so dear to a parent worn out by age

latin: una caput seri nata nepotis alit,
english: does an only daughter rear the head of a late grandson,
note: caput: head, i.e. the person (the child).

latin: qui, cum divitiis vix tandem inventus avitis
english: who, when, found at last scarcely for the ancestral riches,
note: divitiis avitis: dative, an heir for the grandfather's wealth.

latin: nomen testatas intulit in tabulas,
english: has brought his name into the witnessed tablets,
note: testatas tabulas: the attested will.

latin: impia derisi gentilis gaudia tollens
english: taking away the impious joys of the mocked kinsman,
note: gentilis: clansman who hoped to inherit.

latin: suscitat a cano vulturium capiti:
english: rouses the vulture from the grey head:
note: Metaphor: the legacy-hunter (vulture) is driven off from the old man.

latin: nec tantum niveo gavisa est ulla columbo
english: nor so much did any rejoice in her snowy dove
note: columbo: male dove; gavisa est (perfect).

latin: compar, quae multo dicitur improbius
english: mate, who is said much more shamelessly

latin: oscula mordenti semper decerpere rostro
english: kisses with biting beak always to pluck

latin: quam quae praecipue multivola est mulier:
english: than she who is especially a much-desiring woman:
note: multivola: wanting many (lovers).

latin: sed tu horum magnos vicisti sola furores,
english: but you alone surpassed the great frenzies of these,
note: horum: masculine/neuter plural genitive, of these (examples).

latin: ut semel es flavo conciliata viro.
english: once you were joined to your golden-haired husband.
note: ut semel: as soon as, once.

latin: aut nihil aut paulo cui tum concedere digna
english: to whom then worthy to yield either nothing or a little
note: cui: dative, Laodamia; the beloved yields to her not at all or only a little.

latin: lux mea se nostrum contulit in gremium,
english: my light betook herself into our lap,
note: lux mea: the beloved (Lesbia). nostrum: 'our' for 'my'.

latin: quam circumcursans hinc illinc saepe Cupido
english: whom, running around this way and that, often Cupid

latin: fulgebat crocina candidus in tunica.
english: shone, bright in a saffron tunic.
note: quam (93) is the object of circumcursans (running around her).

latin: quae tamenetsi uno non est contenta Catullo,
english: who, although with one is not content Catullus,
note: uno ... Catullo: ablative, 'with Catullus alone'.

latin: rara verecundae furta feremus erae,
english: the rare thefts of my modest mistress we will bear,
note: furta: stolen love, infidelities (metaphor).

latin: ne nimium simus stultorum more molesti:
english: lest we be too troublesome in the manner of fools:

latin: saepe etiam Iuno, maxima caelicolum,
english: often even Juno, greatest of the heaven-dwellers,

latin: coniugis in culpa flagrantem concoquit iram
english: at her husband's fault digests her blazing wrath,
note: concoquit: digests (metaphor), i.e. swallows, suppresses her anger.

latin: noscens omnivoli plurima furta Iovis.
english: knowing the very many thefts of all-desiring Jove.
note: furta: stolen loves (metaphor).

latin: atqui nec divis homines componier aequum est
english: And yet it is not fair for men to be compared with gods
note: componier: archaic passive infinitive (= componi).
Merrill marks a lacuna of uncertain extent after 101; the gap marker is kept.
Lacuna continued; the gap marker is kept.

latin: ingratum tremuli tolle parentis onus.
english: take away the thankless burden of a trembling parent.
note: Sense uncertain because of the preceding lacuna; perhaps the poet tells himself to drop the role of a fussing, jealous old father.

latin: nec tamen illa mihi dextra deducta paterna
english: Nor yet she to me, led by a father's right hand,
note: Not brought as a bride in a formal wedding.

latin: fragrantem Assyrio venit odore domum,
english: came to a house fragrant with Assyrian scent,

latin: sed furtiva dedit mira munuscula nocte
english: but in a stealthy night gave wondrous little gifts,
note: furtiva: taken with nocte; munuscula: little gifts, i.e. her favours.

latin: ipsius ex ipso dempta viri gremio.
english: taken from the very lap of her husband himself.
note: ipsius viri: her own husband.

latin: quare illud satis est, si nobis is datur unis
english: Wherefore this is enough, if to us alone is given that one
note: is ... quem diem (107-108): that day which.

latin: quem lapide illa diem candidiore notat.
english: day which she marks with a whiter stone.
note: Metaphor: a white stone marked a lucky day.

latin: hoc tibi quod potui confectum carmine munus
english: This gift, made up in song as I could, to you

latin: pro multis, Alli, redditur officiis,
english: for many services, Allius, is rendered,

latin: ne vestrum scabra tangat robigine nomen
english: lest your name with scaly rust may touch
note: vestrum: 'your' (plural, Allius and his household). The subject of tangat is in line 112.

latin: haec atque illa dies atque alia atque alia.
english: this and that day and another and another.
note: Metaphor: time as rust on a name.

latin: huc addent divi quam plurima, quae Themis olim
english: To this the gods will add as many as possible, which Themis once
note: quam plurima: as many (gifts) as possible.

latin: antiquis solita est munera ferre piis:
english: was accustomed to bring as gifts to the pious of old:

latin: sitis felices et tu simul et tua vita
english: may you be happy, both you and together your life,
note: tua vita: your beloved.

latin: et domus, in qua nos lusimus et domina,
english: and the house, in which we played, and the mistress,
note: lusimus: played (at love). domina: the beloved, or the mistress of the house; disputed.

latin: et qui principio nobis † terram dedit aufert,
english: and he who in the beginning to us † gave the land takes away,
note: The line is corrupt (marked † in Merrill); the words terram dedit aufert are rendered literally and make no sure sense. Many emendations exist (e.g. te tradidit Anser), none certain.

latin: a quo sunt primo omnia nata bona,
english: from whom first all good things were born,

latin: et longe ante omnes mihi quae me carior ipso est,
english: and far before all she who is dearer to me than myself,

latin: lux mea, qua viva vivere dulce mihi est.
english: my light, with whom living, to live is sweet to me.
note: qua viva: ablative absolute, 'while she lives'.

latin: Noli admirari quare tibi femina nulla,
english: Do not wonder why to you no woman,

latin: Rufe, velit tenerum supposuisse femur,
english: Rufus, wishes to have put her tender thigh beneath,
note: supposuisse femur: to have placed her thigh under (you), i.e. to have sex with you.

latin: non si illam rarae labefactes munere vestis
english: not if you should loosen her with the gift of a rare garment
note: labefactes: shake, loosen, i.e. try to overcome her resistance.

latin: aut perluciduli deliciis lapidis.
english: or with the delights of a clear little stone.
note: perluciduli lapidis: a transparent gem.

latin: laedit te quaedam mala fabula, qua tibi fertur
english: A certain bad tale harms you, by which it is said that for you
note: fertur: is said, rumoured.

latin: valle sub alarum trux habitare caper.
english: under the valley of the armpits lives a fierce goat.
note: Metaphor: goat = rank armpit smell.

latin: hunc metuunt omnes. neque mirum: nam mala valde est
english: Him all fear. Nor is it a wonder: for very bad is

latin: bestia, nec quicum bella puella cubet.
english: the beast, nor one with whom a pretty girl would lie.
note: quicum: with whom (masculine/neuter, = the beast).

latin: quare aut crudelem nasorum interfice pestem,
english: Therefore either kill the cruel plague of noses,

latin: aut admirari desine cur fugiunt.
english: or stop wondering why they flee.

latin: Nulli se dicit mulier mea nubere malle
english: To no one says my woman she would rather be married
note: nulli ... nubere: to marry (dative of the man married).

latin: quam mihi, non si se Iuppiter ipse petat.
english: than to me, not if Jupiter himself should seek her.
note: mihi is dative after nubere; 'to' is supplied.

latin: dicit: sed mulier cupido quod dicit amanti
english: She says: but what a woman says to an eager lover

latin: in vento et rapida scribere oportet aqua.
english: in wind and in rapid water it is right to write.
note: oportet: it is proper, one ought.

latin: Si cui iure bono sacer alarum obstitit hircus,
english: If to anyone by good right the accursed goat of the armpits has been an obstacle,
note: sacer: accursed. hircus: he-goat, i.e. armpit stench.

latin: aut si quem merito tarda podagra secat,
english: or if anyone deservedly slow gout cuts,
note: tarda podagra: gout that slows, lames.

latin: Aemulus iste tuus, qui vestrum exercet amorem,
english: that rival of yours, who exercises your love,
note: vestrum amorem: the love of you two (the addressee and his woman).

latin: mirifice est a te nactus utrumque malum.
english: wonderfully has from you obtained both evils.
note: a te: 'from you'; the sense of the line is disputed (perhaps 'has caught both from you').

latin: nam quotiens futuit totiens ulciscitur ambos:
english: For as often as he fucks, so often he punishes both:
note: futuit: fucks.

latin: illam adfligit odore, ipse perit podagra.
english: her he strikes with the smell, he himself perishes with gout.

latin: Dicebas quondam solum te nosse Catullum,
english: You used to say once that you knew only Catullus,
note: nosse: to know, also in the sexual sense.

latin: Lesbia, nec prae me velle tenere Iovem.
english: Lesbia, and did not wish before me to hold Jove.
note: prae me: in preference to me.

latin: dilexi tum te non tantum ut vulgus amicam,
english: I loved you then not only as the crowd a girlfriend,
note: non tantum: 'not only'.

latin: sed pater ut gnatos diligit et generos.
english: but as a father loves his sons and sons-in-law.

latin: nunc te cognovi: quare etsi impensius uror,
english: Now I have come to know you: therefore although more vehemently I burn,

latin: multo mi tamen es vilior et levior.
english: much to me nevertheless you are cheaper and lighter.
note: mi = mihi.

latin: qui potis est? inquis. quod amantem iniuria talis
english: How is that possible? you say. Because an injury such as this the lover
note: qui potis est: how can that be; the question is the addressee's, introduced by inquis.

latin: cogit amare magis, sed bene velle minus.
english: compels to love more, but to wish well less.
note: bene velle: to wish well, i.e. to feel goodwill and esteem.

latin: Desine de quoquam quicquam bene velle mereri
english: Stop wishing of anyone in anything to deserve well
note: de quoquam bene mereri: to earn gratitude from anyone.

latin: aut aliquem fieri posse putare pium.
english: or to think that anyone can become dutiful.
note: pium: grateful, loyal.

latin: omnia sunt ingrata, nihil fecisse benigne:
english: All things are thankless, nothing to have done kindly:
note: nihil fecisse benigne: to have acted kindly counts for nothing.

latin: immo etiam taedet, taedet obestque magis:
english: rather even it wearies, wearies and harms more:

latin: ut mihi, quem nemo gravius nec acerbius urget
english: as with me, whom no one more heavily nor more bitterly presses

latin: Quam modo qui me unum atque unicum amicum habuit.
english: than he who just now held me as his one and only friend.

latin: Gellius audierat patruum obiurgare solere,
english: Gellius had heard that his uncle was accustomed to rebuke,
note: patruus: father's brother, proverbially a stern moralist.

latin: si quis delicias diceret aut faceret.
english: if anyone spoke or did naughty things.
note: delicias: love-play, sexual frolics.

latin: hoc ne ipsi accideret, patrui perdepsuit ipsam
english: So that this would not happen to himself, he thoroughly kneaded his uncle's very
note: perdepsuit: thoroughly kneaded, i.e. fucked; its object uxorem is in line 4.

latin: uxorem et patruum reddidit Harpocratem.
english: wife, and rendered his uncle a Harpocrates.
note: Harpocrates: Egyptian god of silence, shown with finger on lips.

latin: quod voluit fecit: nam, quamvis irrumet ipsum
english: What he wanted he did: for, although he should mouth-fuck the very
note: irrumet: to fuck in the mouth (force to fellate).

latin: nunc patruum, verbum non faciet patruus.
english: uncle himself now, a word the uncle will not make.
note: ipsum (line 5) = the uncle himself.

latin: Huc est mens deducta tua, mea Lesbia, culpa,
english: To this point has my mind been brought down, my Lesbia, by your fault,
note: tua culpa: ablative, through your fault.

latin: atque ita se officio perdidit ipsa suo,
english: and so has ruined itself by its own devotion,
note: officio: its dutiful service, loyalty.

latin: ut iam nec bene velle queat tibi, si optuma fias,
english: that now it could neither wish you well, if you became the best,
note: bene velle: feel goodwill, esteem.

latin: nec desistere amare, omnia si facias.
english: nor cease to love, if you did everything.
note: omnia si facias: whatever (bad) you might do.

latin: Si qua recordanti benefacta priora voluptas
english: If any pleasure in recalling former good deeds

latin: est homini, cum se cogitat esse pium,
english: there is for a man, when he reflects that he is dutiful,
note: pium: dutiful, loyal.

latin: nec sanctam violasse fidem, nec foedere in ullo
english: nor has violated sacred faith, nor in any compact

latin: divum ad fallendos numine abusum homines,
english: abused the divine power of the gods to deceive men,
note: divum: genitive plural, of the gods.

latin: multa parata manent in longa aetate, Catulle,
english: many remain prepared in long life, Catullus,

latin: ex hoc ingrato gaudia amore tibi.
english: from this unthankful love, joys for you.

latin: nam quaecumque homines bene cuiquam aut dicere possunt
english: For whatever men to anyone can either say well

latin: aut facere, haec a te dictaque factaque sunt:
english: or do, these by you have been both said and done:

latin: omnia quae ingratae perierunt credita menti.
english: all which, entrusted to an unthankful mind, have perished.
note: credita: entrusted, like money lent (metaphor).

latin: quare cur tu te iam amplius excrucies?
english: Therefore why should you torture yourself now any further?

latin: quin tu animo offirmas atque istinc teque reducis
english: Why not make firm in your mind and lead yourself back from there,
note: quin: why not. istinc: from where you are.

latin: et dis invitis desinis esse miser?
english: and, with the gods unwilling, cease to be wretched?
note: dis invitis: the gods being unwilling, i.e. since the gods do not want your misery.

latin: difficile est longum subito deponere amorem;
english: It is difficult suddenly to lay down a long love;

latin: difficile est, verum hoc qua libet efficias.
english: it is difficult, but this by whatever way you please you should accomplish.
note: qua libet: by whatever way it pleases.

latin: una salus haec est, hoc est tibi pervincendum;
english: This is the one safety, this must be fought through by you;
note: salus: safety, salvation.

latin: hoc facias, sive id non pote sive pote.
english: this you should do, whether it is not possible or possible.
note: pote = potest (or potis est).

latin: o di, si vestrum est misereri, aut si quibus unquam
english: O gods, if it is yours to pity, or if to any ever

latin: extremam iam ipsa in morte tulistis opem,
english: at the very point of death you have brought final help,

latin: me miserum adspicite et, si vitam puriter egi,
english: look on wretched me and, if I have lived my life cleanly,

latin: eripite hanc pestem perniciemque mihi!
english: snatch away this plague and ruin from me!

latin: hei mihi subrepens imos ut torpor in artus
english: alas for me, creeping beneath into my lowest limbs like a torpor,
note: hei mihi: Merrill's reading (others quae mihi); the subject is the pestis of line 20. ut torpor: like a numbness.

latin: expulit ex omni pectore laetitias.
english: it has driven out from all my breast joys.
note: 'it' is supplied for the subject (the plague).

latin: non iam illud quaero, contra ut me diligat illa,
english: Not now this do I seek, that in return she should love me,
note: illa (she) stands at the end of the Latin line.

latin: aut, quod non potis est, esse pudica velit:
english: or, which is not possible, that she should wish to be chaste:
note: pudica: chaste, faithful.

latin: ipse valere opto et taetrum hunc deponere morbum.
english: I myself wish to be well and to lay down this foul disease.
note: Metaphor: love as a sickness.

latin: o di, reddite mi hoc pro pietate mea.
english: O gods, give back to me this in return for my piety.

latin: Rufe mihi frustra ac nequiquam credite amice
english: Rufus, to me in vain and to no purpose believed friend,
note: credite amice: vocatives, 'trusted friend'.

latin: (frustra? immo magno cum pretio atque malo),
english: (in vain? no, rather at a great price and harm),
note: The parenthesis is in the Latin.

latin: sicine subrepsti mi atque intestina perurens
english: is it thus you crept beneath me and, burning through my entrails,
note: subrepsti = subrepsisti: crept up on, stole in upon.

latin: hei misero eripuisti omnia nostra bona?
english: alas, from wretched me snatched away all our goods?
note: nostra: 'our' for 'my'.

latin: eripuisti, eheu nostrae crudele venenum
english: You snatched them, alas, cruel poison of our

latin: vitae, eheu nostrae pestis amicitiae.
english: life, alas, plague of our friendship.

latin: Gallus habet fratres, quorum est lepidissima coniunx
english: Gallus has brothers, of whom there is a most charming wife

latin: alterius, lepidus filius alterius.
english: of one, a charming son of the other.

latin: Gallus homo est bellus: nam dulces iungit amores,
english: Gallus is a pretty man: for he joins sweet loves,
note: bellus: pretty, fine (ironic).

latin: cum puero ut bello bella puella cubet.
english: so that with a pretty boy a pretty girl may lie.

latin: Gallus homo est stultus nec se videt esse maritum,
english: Gallus is a stupid man, nor sees himself to be a husband,

latin: qui patruus patrui monstret adulterium.
english: who as uncle shows an uncle's adultery.
note: He teaches his nephew how to cuckold an uncle, though he is himself a husband and an uncle.
Merrill marks a lacuna here; the gap marker is kept. Lines 7-10 are usually printed as a separate fragment (78b).
Lacuna continued; the gap marker is kept.

latin: Sed nunc id doleo quod purae pura puellae
english: But now I grieve at this, that of a pure girl pure

latin: savia comminxit spurca saliva tua.
english: kisses your filthy spittle has pissed on.
note: comminxit: urinated upon, defiled. savia: kisses (object); saliva tua is the subject.

latin: verum id non impune feres: nam te omnia saecla
english: But this you will not carry off unpunished: for you all ages

latin: noscent et qui sis fama loquetur anus.
english: will know, and who you are Fame, an old woman, will tell.
note: fama anus: rumour grown old, i.e. lasting into the future.

latin: Lesbius est pulcher: quid ni? quem Lesbia malit
english: Lesbius is pretty: why not? whom Lesbia would prefer
note: pulcher: a pun on the cognomen Pulcher; Lesbius is usually taken as P. Clodius Pulcher, Clodia's brother.

latin: quam te cum tota gente, Catulle, tua.
english: to you with all your family, Catullus.

latin: sed tamen hic pulcher vendat cum gente Catullum,
english: But yet let this pretty one sell Catullus with his family,
note: cum gente: with his (Catullus') clan.

latin: si tria notorum savia reppererit.
english: if he finds three kisses of acquaintances.
note: notorum savia: kisses from people who know him, implying his mouth is defiled; sense debated.

latin: Quid dicam, Gelli, quare rosea ista labella
english: What shall I say, Gellius, why those rosy little lips

latin: Hiberna fiant candidiora nive,
english: become whiter than winter snow,

latin: mane domo cum exis et cum te octava quiete
english: in the morning when you go out from home and when you, from rest, the eighth
note: te ... octava quiete / e molli ... hora: the eighth hour (early afternoon) rouses you from soft rest on the long (summer) day.

latin: e molli longo suscitat hora die?
english: out of soft, on the long day, hour rouses?
note: e molli: 'from soft (rest)'; quiete stands in line 3.

latin: nescio quid certe est: an vere fama susurrat
english: Something there certainly is: or does rumour truly whisper

latin: grandia te medii tenta vorare viri?
english: that you devour the big stiff things of a man's middle?
note: grandia tenta: the big taut (members), i.e. an erect penis; the charge is fellatio.

latin: sic certe est: clamant Victoris rupta miselli
english: So it certainly is: they shout, poor little Victor's burst
note: Victoris miselli: of wretched little Victor.

latin: ilia, et emulso labra notata sero.
english: loins, and lips marked with milked-out whey.
note: ilia: groin, flanks. emulso sero: milked-out whey, i.e. semen.

latin: Nemone in tanto potuit populo esse, Iuventi,
english: Could there be no one in so great a people, Juventius,
note: Nemone: interrogative, 'was there not anyone'.

latin: bellus homo quem tu diligere inciperes
english: a pretty man whom you might begin to love

latin: praeterquam iste tuus moribunda ab sede Pisauri
english: besides that one of yours from the dying seat of Pisaurum
note: moribunda sede: Pisaurum (Pesaro), a decayed, unhealthy town.

latin: hospes inaurata pallidior statua?
english: guest, paler than a gilded statue?
note: hospes: guest, friend from abroad.

latin: qui tibi nunc cordi est, quem tu praeponere nobis
english: who is now dear to your heart, whom you to set before us
note: cordi est: is to (your) heart, is dear. nobis: 'us' for 'me'.

latin: audes et nescis quod facinus facias.
english: dare, and you do not know what a crime you are committing.
